title: Moral Luck and Responsibility
subtitle: Can you deserve blame for what was never in your control?
objectives: By the end you will be able to state the Control Principle and explain why moral luck seems to contradict it.
By the end you will be able to distinguish Nagel's four kinds of moral luck (resultant, circumstantial, constitutive and causal) with an example of each.
By the end you will be able to explain Williams's Gauguin case and his notion of agent-regret.
By the end you will be able to describe Strawson's reactive attitudes and how they reframe the problem of responsibility.
By the end you will be able to evaluate the main responses to moral luck, from denial to acceptance.
hook:
Two friends leave a party at the same time. Both have had a few drinks too many; both feel fine; both drive home along the same dark road at the same speed. Neither is more careless than the other. On the first driver's route, nothing happens. On the second's, a child chases a ball into the road, and the child dies.

The first driver wakes up with a headache and a twinge of guilt. The second faces a prison sentence, the hatred of a family, and a lifetime of remorse. Most of us feel that the second driver has done something far worse. Yet the only difference between them is something neither controlled: whether a child happened to run into the road. If we blame people only for what they control, the two deserve exactly the same blame. If we blame the second more, we are letting **luck** decide moral worth. This puzzle, named by Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel in a famous pair of papers in 1976, is the problem of **moral luck**.

sections.heading: The Control Principle and Kant's Jewel
sections.body:
Much of our thinking about blame rests on an intuitive rule that philosophers call the **Control Principle**: we are morally assessable only for what is due to factors under our control. If someone pushes you into a bystander, you did not harm the bystander in any blameworthy sense; you were the instrument, not the agent. Excuses like "I didn't know," "I was forced" and "it was an accident" all appeal to this principle.

The principle's most powerful champion is Kant (Day 56). In the *Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals* (1785), Kant argued that the only thing good without qualification is a **good will**: the will to do one's duty because it is one's duty. Its worth does not depend on what it achieves. Even if, through misfortune, a good will accomplished nothing at all, Kant wrote that it would still shine like a jewel, as something having its full worth in itself. Morality, on this view, is precisely the domain that luck cannot reach. Your health, wealth, talent and success are hostage to fortune; your moral worth is not.

This picture is deeply attractive, and it is not only Kant's. Any religious or secular tradition that promises that everyone, whatever their circumstances, has an equal chance to be good draws on the same thought. The Stoics (Days 25 and 26) taught something similar: virtue depends entirely on what is "up to us."

The trouble, as Williams and Nagel showed, is that our actual moral judgments break the Control Principle constantly. And when we try to apply it consistently, it threatens to leave nothing to judge at all.

sections.heading: Nagel's Four Kinds of Moral Luck
sections.body:
Thomas Nagel's paper "Moral Luck" (1976, reprinted in *Mortal Questions*, 1979) defines moral luck this way: it occurs when a significant aspect of what someone does depends on factors beyond their control, yet we continue to treat them as an object of moral judgment. He distinguished four kinds.

**1. Resultant luck: luck in how things turn out.** The drunk drivers are an example. Others: two would-be assassins fire at a politician; one bullet hits, the other is deflected by a passing bird. One is a murderer, the other guilty only of attempted murder, and most legal systems punish them differently. A doctor makes a risky call that saves the patient and is praised as bold; the same call that fails is condemned as reckless. Nagel notes that we often cannot know whether a decision was justified until we see its result.

**2. Circumstantial luck: luck in the situations you face.** Nagel's most chilling example: ordinary citizens of Nazi Germany had an opportunity to behave heroically by opposing the regime, and most behaved badly instead. People in other countries, who would perhaps have behaved just as badly in the same position, never faced the test. They are not culpable for what they never did, yet their real character might be no better. Most of us have never been tested in such ways, and we do not know how we would fare.

**3. Constitutive luck: luck in who you are.** Your temperament, inclinations, talents and capacities were shaped by genes, upbringing and experiences you did not choose. Someone who is naturally envious or cowardly is blamed for being envious or cowardly, even though they did not choose their nature. Someone with a placid, generous disposition finds kindness easy and is praised for it.

**4. Causal luck: luck in how you are determined by antecedent circumstances.** This is the classical problem of free will (the Mind track takes it up in Lesson 3). If every choice is the outcome of prior causes reaching back before your birth, then nothing at all is ultimately under your control.

Put these together and the result is alarming. Nagel wrote that the area of genuine agency "seems to shrink under this scrutiny to an extensionless point." If we apply the Control Principle consistently, almost nothing we do is assessable. If we abandon it, we seem to accept that moral standing is a lottery. Nagel did not claim to solve the problem. He argued that it arises from a clash between two standpoints we cannot give up: the internal view of ourselves as agents, and the external view of ourselves as parts of the world, where everything that happens is a matter of events, not deeds.

sections.heading: Williams: Gauguin and Agent-Regret
sections.body:
Bernard Williams's paper of the same title approached the problem from another direction. His concern was less with blame than with **justification**, and with the Kantian hope that a rational person could make a life immune to luck.

His central example is a stylized painter he calls Gauguin, loosely based on the real artist. Gauguin abandons his wife and children, causing them real hardship, to go to Tahiti and pursue his painting. Was he justified? Williams's answer is startling: whether Gauguin's choice was justified depends on whether he succeeds as a painter, and that is something he could not know when he chose. If he becomes a great artist, he may be able to look back and be glad of his decision. If he fails, he has no justification at all; he simply abandoned his family for nothing.

Crucially, Williams distinguishes two kinds of failure. If Gauguin is injured on the voyage and never paints, that is **extrinsic** luck: the project failed for reasons outside him, and the question of his justification never gets settled. But if he arrives and turns out to lack the talent, that is **intrinsic** luck: the failure lies in the project and in him, and it shows that the choice was unjustified. This suggests that rational justification itself can depend on luck, which is exactly what Kant's picture denies.

Williams's second contribution is the notion of **agent-regret**. He imagines a lorry driver who, through no fault of his own, runs over a child. A spectator can regret the death; anyone can wish it had not happened. But the driver feels something different: a first-personal regret about his own part in it, even though he was not at fault. Williams argued that this feeling is not irrational. Indeed, we would think less of a driver who said, "Not my fault, so not my concern." We expect him to try to make some kind of amends.

The lesson: our responsibility extends beyond what we intend and control. Agent-regret recognizes that we are agents in a world, whose actions have consequences that become part of our lives. A moral outlook that left this out, Williams thought, would misdescribe what it is to be a human agent.

sections.heading: Strawson's Reactive Attitudes
sections.body:
In 1962, a decade before the moral luck debate, P. F. Strawson delivered a British Academy lecture, "Freedom and Resentment," that changed how philosophers think about responsibility. It offers a different perspective on the whole problem.

Strawson began not with metaphysics but with how we actually relate to one another. We have **reactive attitudes**: resentment when someone injures us, gratitude when they help us, indignation when they wrong a third party, guilt or shame when we wrong others, forgiveness, love, hurt feelings. These attitudes are reactions to the *quality of will* others show toward us: whether they display goodwill, ill will or indifference.

Notice how excuses work. When someone steps on your hand, you feel resentment. If you learn they were pushed, or did not see you, your resentment fades. Such pleas do not suggest the person is not responsible at all; they show that, in this case, no ill will was involved. Strawson contrasts these with **exempting** conditions: "He's only a child," "She's not herself; she's in a psychotic episode." These lead us to suspend the reactive attitudes and adopt instead what Strawson called the **objective attitude**, seeing the person as someone to be managed, treated or trained rather than reasoned with.

His key move was this. Philosophers asked whether determinism (causal luck) would make all reactive attitudes irrational. Strawson replied that the question misunderstands their role. Our commitment to participating in human relationships, with all the reactive attitudes they involve, is too deep to be given up because of a general theoretical belief. We could not seriously adopt the objective attitude toward everyone, all the time, and if we could, life would be unrecognizably impoverished. Responsibility, on this view, is not a metaphysical fact waiting for the free will debate to confirm it; it is grounded in the practices of holding one another responsible.

This has implications for moral luck. If reactive attitudes respond to quality of will, then the two drunk drivers showed the same quality of will and deserve the same resentment. But reactions are also shaped by what actually happened, and Strawson's naturalism can explain, though perhaps not justify, why the death changes how everyone, including the driver, feels.

Gary Watson (1987) pressed Strawson's view with a real case: Robert Harris, who murdered two teenagers in California in 1978 and was executed in 1992. Harris's crimes inspire intense indignation. But when we learn of the extreme abuse he suffered as a child, our reactive attitudes waver. Watson argued that this shows the attitudes are sensitive to the question of how a person came to be as they are: to constitutive luck.

sections.heading: Responses: Deny, Explain or Accept
sections.body:
What should we conclude? Philosophers have tried three broad strategies.

**Deny moral luck.** Some argue that, properly understood, the two drivers *are* equally blameworthy. Michael Zimmerman, for instance, argues that what we deserve depends on what we would freely have done in other circumstances. The lucky driver is as culpable as the unlucky one; he simply has not been caught out by the world. This preserves the Control Principle, but at a price: it seems to imply that a peaceful citizen who would have become a Nazi collaborator in 1930s Germany is as blameworthy as one who did, which strikes many as unfair in a new way.

**Explain it away.** Others say the difference in our responses is not a difference in blameworthiness but in something else. Outcomes give us **evidence** about how careless someone really was (Norvin Richards). Or we should distinguish how much someone *deserves* blame from how much we *should* respond, for instance by compensating victims or punishing to deter. On this view, the law may reasonably punish the lucky and unlucky driver differently for practical reasons, while their moral blameworthiness is the same.

**Accept it.** A third group, inspired by Williams, accepts that luck shapes moral life and asks how to live well with this fact. Margaret Urban Walker argued that the ideal of a "pure" agent, responsible only for what it fully controls, is a fantasy, and that the virtues of a mature agent include taking responsibility for more than one controls. Susan Wolf (2001) suggested that there is a nameless virtue: the disposition to take responsibility for the unforeseen results of one's actions, as the lorry driver does. Someone who said "I was merely unlucky" after killing a child would show a defect of character, even if the claim was literally true.

No strategy is costless. Denial makes us blameworthy for countless things we never did. Explaining away risks treating our deepest reactions as mistakes. Acceptance seems to abandon the ideal of fairness that made the Control Principle attractive in the first place. As with so many problems in this track, the best answer may depend on which costs you can live with.

keyQuote.text: The area of genuine agency, and therefore of legitimate moral judgment, seems to shrink under this scrutiny to an extensionless point.
keyQuote.source: Thomas Nagel, 'Moral Luck' (1976), in Mortal Questions (1979)

modernConnection.title: Outcome Bias: Judging Decisions by How They Turn Out
modernConnection.body:
Psychologists have shown that moral luck is not just a philosopher's puzzle but a measurable feature of human judgment. In a 1988 study, Jonathan Baron and John Hershey gave people descriptions of medical decisions made under uncertainty. The decisions were identical; only the outcomes differed. People consistently rated the very same decision as better, and the decision-maker as more competent, when it happened to turn out well. They called this **outcome bias**.

Fiery Cushman (2008) found a revealing split. When people were asked whether an act was *wrong* or whether its agent was a bad person, they relied mostly on the agent's intentions and beliefs. But when asked how much the agent should be *blamed* or *punished*, the outcome mattered a great deal: an unlucky agent who caused harm was punished more than an identical agent who did not. This fits closely with the "explain it away" strategy from this lesson: perhaps we hold two different kinds of judgment, one tracking quality of will (Strawson) and one tracking harm caused.

Outcome bias matters in daily life. Poker players and decision theorists have a name for the mistake of judging a choice by its result: **resulting**, popularized by Annie Duke in *Thinking in Bets* (2018). A sports coach who makes a statistically sound call that fails is fired; one who makes a reckless call that works is hailed as a genius. Doctors, investors and managers are evaluated, rewarded and sued on outcomes they did not fully control. And on social media, one unlucky moment, a careless joke that went viral, can define a person's public reputation while thousands of others who did the same thing go unnoticed.

The philosophy of moral luck does not tell us simply to ignore outcomes. Williams would remind us that outcomes really do become part of who we are. But it does help us ask a useful question when we judge: are we responding to what this person chose, or only to what happened?

vocabulary.definition: The phenomenon of a person being morally judged for something that depends significantly on factors beyond their control.
vocabulary.example: The unlucky drunk driver who kills a child, compared with an equally careless driver who arrives home safely, is a case of moral luck.

vocabulary.definition: The principle that people are morally assessable only for what is due to factors under their control.
vocabulary.example: The Control Principle says you should not be blamed for harm you caused when someone else pushed you.

vocabulary.definition: Luck in the way one's actions turn out.
vocabulary.example: Two assassins who fire with identical skill, only one of whom hits, differ by resultant luck.

vocabulary.definition: Luck in the situations and moral tests one happens to face.
vocabulary.example: A person never asked to resist a tyrannical regime is spared a test by circumstantial luck.

vocabulary.definition: Luck in the kind of person one is: one's temperament, capacities and character, as shaped by factors one did not choose.
vocabulary.example: Someone with an easygoing disposition finds patience easy partly through constitutive luck.

vocabulary.definition: Williams's term for the distinctive first-person regret felt by someone about their own part in a harm, even when they were not at fault.
vocabulary.example: The lorry driver who blamelessly hits a child feels agent-regret that no bystander shares.

vocabulary.definition: Strawson's term for emotional responses to others' quality of will, such as resentment, gratitude and indignation.
vocabulary.example: Your resentment at a friend who betrayed a secret is one of the reactive attitudes.

vocabulary.definition: Strawson's term for viewing a person as something to be managed, treated or handled, rather than as a participant in reciprocal moral relationships.
vocabulary.example: We adopt the objective attitude toward a small child who bites, rather than resenting them.

thinkingExercise.title: Your Own Lottery
thinkingExercise.prompt: Examine the role luck has played in your own moral record.
steps: Recall a time when you did something careless that turned out fine (a near miss while driving, a remark that could have hurt someone). How would you judge yourself if it had turned out badly?
Identify one moral test you have never faced, and honestly ask how you think you would have done. What does this suggest about circumstantial luck?
List three traits of your character you are proud of. For each, write down the factors outside your control that helped shape it.
Decide which response to moral luck (deny, explain away, or accept) you find most persuasive. Apply it to the two drunk drivers: what should each feel, and what should happen to each?
Reflect on Susan Wolf's suggestion: is there a virtue in taking responsibility for more than you strictly controlled? When might it become excessive?

summary: The Control Principle says we are assessable only for what we control; Kant's good will, which shines like a jewel whatever its results, is the classic expression of this ideal.
Nagel identified four kinds of moral luck (resultant, circumstantial, constitutive and causal) and warned that applying the Control Principle consistently would leave almost nothing to judge.
Williams's Gauguin case suggests that even rational justification may depend on how things turn out, and his notion of agent-regret shows our responsibility exceeds our control.
Strawson grounded responsibility in reactive attitudes responsive to quality of will, arguing that our participation in them is too deep to be overturned by theoretical worries like determinism.

Responses to moral luck include denying it (equal blame for the lucky and unlucky), explaining it away (outcomes as evidence, or practical rather than moral differences), and accepting it as part of mature agency.

quiz.question: Two equally careful hikers both start campfires; one is caught by a sudden wind and causes a forest fire. Which kind of moral luck does this illustrate?
quiz.explanation: The hikers differ only in how things turned out, which is resultant luck.

quiz.question: What does the Control Principle say?
options: We are morally assessable only for what is due to factors under our control
We are responsible for all the consequences of our actions
quiz.explanation: It is the intuitive rule behind ordinary excuses: no blame for what one could not control.

quiz.question: Kant held that a good will's value depends on whether it succeeds in achieving its aims.
quiz.explanation: Kant held the reverse: even if a good will achieved nothing, it would shine like a jewel, with its full worth in itself.

quiz.question: Nagel's example of citizens in Nazi Germany who behaved badly, compared with people elsewhere who would have done the same but were never tested, illustrates:
quiz.explanation: The difference lies in the circumstances each person happened to face.

quiz.question: According to Williams, what would show that Gauguin's choice was unjustified?
options: Being injured on the voyage before painting
Arriving in Tahiti and turning out to lack the talent to succeed
quiz.explanation: That is intrinsic luck: the failure lies in the project itself. An injury on the voyage would be extrinsic and would leave the question of justification unsettled.

quiz.question: Williams thought that a lorry driver who blamelessly kills a child is irrational to feel any special regret, since he was not at fault.
quiz.explanation: Williams argued that agent-regret is appropriate, and that we would think less of a driver who felt nothing beyond a spectator's regret.

quiz.question: For Strawson, learning that someone who stepped on your hand was pushed causes your resentment to fade because:
options: It shows they did not display ill will in this case
It shows they are not a responsible agent at all
quiz.explanation: This is an excusing condition: it changes our view of the quality of will in the act, not of the person's status as an agent.

quiz.question: Strawson argued that our commitment to the reactive attitudes is too deep to be abandoned merely because of a general theoretical belief in determinism.
quiz.explanation: He held that we could not seriously adopt the objective attitude toward everyone, and that responsibility is grounded in these interpersonal practices.

quiz.question: A manager is fired for a well-reasoned investment that lost money because of an unpredictable crash. Which psychological finding does this illustrate?
quiz.explanation: Outcome bias is judging a decision by its result rather than by the quality of the reasoning when it was made.

goDeeper.body:
One of the most interesting developments in this debate concerns the law. Criminal law around the world embodies resultant luck: murder is punished more harshly than attempted murder, and dangerous driving that kills is treated far more severely than the same driving that does not. Some legal theorists, such as Andrew Ashworth and Larry Alexander, argue for a **subjectivist** reform: punish according to culpability, which depends on intention and risk-taking, not on results. The American Model Penal Code moved some way in this direction by grading most attempts at the same level as the completed offense, though with exceptions for the most serious crimes.

Defenders of the traditional approach, such as Antony Duff, reply that the law rightly reflects the difference between a wrong done and a wrong merely attempted. A victim's family has suffered a real loss, and a legal system that ignored that loss would fail to take the harm seriously. On this view the criminal law is not only a device for grading culpability but a public response to wrongs, and wrongs depend partly on results.

A second advanced theme connects moral luck to **structural injustice**. Constitutive and circumstantial luck are not distributed randomly: some people are born into poverty, discrimination or violence, which shapes both their opportunities and their characters. Philosophers influenced by Strawson and Watson ask whether our practices of blame adequately recognize this, and whether a society that leaves some people far more exposed to moral tests than others bears part of the responsibility for how they fare. Here the moral luck debate meets the political philosophy of Rawls (Day 82), who argued that no one deserves their place in the natural lottery of talents.

questions: Should the law punish attempted crimes as severely as completed ones? What would be gained and lost?
If constitutive luck shapes everyone's character, does it make sense to be proud of your virtues?
Is Susan Wolf right that there is a virtue in taking responsibility for outcomes you did not control?
